title: How CodeWalk works
description: A walkthrough of this extension's own source: the tour format, the inline bubble player, and how Claude Code is used to generate tours.

steps.title: A walkthrough is just JSON
steps.body:
Everything starts with this shape. A **tour** is a title plus an ordered list of **steps**; each step points at a file and a 1-based line range and carries a Markdown body.

Tours live in `.codewalk/*.tour.json` inside the repo, so they are committed and shared like any other file — exactly what you are reading right now.

steps.title: Surviving edits: re-anchoring
steps.body:
Line numbers rot as code changes. Each step stores the trimmed text of its first line as an `anchor`; when the tour plays, if that line no longer matches we search ±200 lines for it and move the highlight there.

It is cheap and surprisingly effective — most edits shift code rather than rewrite the exact line you anchored on.

steps.title: The bubble is a comment thread
steps.body:
VS Code does not let extensions float arbitrary HTML over the editor, but the **Comments API** gives us an inline, Markdown-capable card attached to a line — which is exactly the website-tour feel we want.

We create one `CommentController` and deny all commenting ranges, so nobody can reply to the bubble; it is purely a display surface.

steps.title: Showing a step
steps.body:
`show()` does the real work: open the document, compute the (possibly re-anchored) range, reveal it centred, then **dispose and recreate** the thread at the last highlighted line.

Recreating rather than moving the thread turned out to be the only reliable way to make the bubble follow the step across files.

steps.title: Spotlight and dimming
steps.body:
Two decoration types: a tinted, left-bordered highlight for the step's lines, and an `opacity: 0.45` decoration applied to everything *else* in the file. Together they read like the dark overlay a web product tour draws around the element it is pointing at.

Both are re-applied whenever visible editors change, so splitting or re-opening the file keeps the spotlight.

steps.title: Asking Claude Code for a tour
steps.body:
Generation is a single prompt to the `claude` CLI. We describe the scope (file, selection, folder, whole repo, or a git diff), the desired depth from the `codewalk.detailLevel` setting, and — most importantly — the exact JSON shape to return.

Claude is given **read-only tools** (`Read, Glob, Grep, LS`) so it can open files itself and verify line numbers rather than guessing.

steps.title: Running the CLI
steps.body:
`claude -p … --output-format json --allowedTools Read,Glob,Grep,LS` runs with the workspace as its working directory. Prompts over ~60 KB (big diffs) are written to a temp file that Claude is told to read, to stay under the OS argument-length limit.

The process is cancellable from the progress notification, and stderr streams into the *CodeWalk* output channel for debugging.

steps.title: Validating what came back
steps.body: LLM output is never trusted blindly. The JSON block is extracted and validated, steps that point at files which do not exist are **dropped**, and an anchor is captured for each surviving step before the tour is written to disk.

steps.title: Wiring it all up
steps.body:
`activate()` creates the player and the sidebar tree, then watches `**/*.tour.json`. Editing a tour file while it is playing hot-reloads the current step, which makes hand-tuning a generated walkthrough pleasant: tweak the JSON, see the bubble update.

That's the whole loop. Press **Next** to finish, or jump around with the status-bar item.
